domains.title: System Design
domains.short_overview: How to design software systems that meet real functional and non-functional requirements under real constraints — from a single request's network path through to production deployment and reliability.

children.title: Requirements
children.short_overview: What a system must do, how well, and under what constraints — decided before any design work starts.

children.title: Functional Requirements
children.short_overview: What the system must actually do — the observable behaviors a user or another system can call and depend on (e.g. 'POST /customers creates a customer').

sections.what: What the system must actually do — the observable behaviors a user or another system can call and depend on (e.g. 'POST /customers creates a customer').
sections.how: Captured as concrete, testable statements, not vague goals. This project's CustomerController endpoints are its functional requirements made real.

children.title: Non-Functional Requirements
children.short_overview: Quality attributes a system must have regardless of specific feature: latency, availability, security, cost, observability — the 'how well', not the 'what'.

sections.what: Quality attributes a system must have regardless of specific feature: latency, availability, security, cost, observability — the 'how well', not the 'what'.
sections.how: Stated as measurable targets (e.g. p99 latency, uptime %) so they can be tested, not left as adjectives like 'fast' or 'scalable'.

children.title: Scale
children.short_overview: The expected volume (requests/sec, data size, concurrent users) a design must handle — determines whether a simple design suffices or a more complex one is justified.

sections.what: The expected volume (requests/sec, data size, concurrent users) a design must handle — determines whether a simple design suffices or a more complex one is justified.
sections.how: Estimate real numbers before designing (back-of-envelope: requests/day / seconds/day = avg QPS, plus a peak multiplier) rather than assuming 'web scale' by default.

children.title: Constraints
children.short_overview: Fixed boundaries a design must work within — budget, team size, existing infrastructure, compliance, deadline — that are not requirements but shape which requirements are even achievable.

sections.what: Fixed boundaries a design must work within — budget, team size, existing infrastructure, compliance, deadline — that are not requirements but shape which requirements are even achievable.
sections.how: This project's own constraints (single-operator budget, no paid infra beyond Railway/Vercel free-ish tiers, no enterprise identity provider) directly shaped its architecture (H2 in-memory DB instead of managed Postgres for the Customer app, no auth layer yet).

children.title: SLO/SLA Concepts
children.short_overview: SLI (a measured indicator, e.g. latency) -> SLO (an internal target for that indicator) -> SLA (an external, often contractual, commitment built on an SLO).

sections.what: SLI (a measured indicator, e.g. latency) -> SLO (an internal target for that indicator) -> SLA (an external, often contractual, commitment built on an SLO).

children.title: Acceptance Criteria
children.short_overview: The explicit, checkable conditions that decide whether a requirement is actually satisfied — the bridge between 'what we want' and 'can we prove it's done'.

sections.what: The explicit, checkable conditions that decide whether a requirement is actually satisfied — the bridge between 'what we want' and 'can we prove it's done'.
sections.how: This project's own Acceptance Contract (agent/acceptance_contract.py) formalizes exactly this idea for AI-driven changes: requirement_id, expected_observable_effect, required_gates, allowed_terminal_outcomes.

children.title: APIs
children.short_overview: The contracts through which independently-deployed systems (or a frontend and backend) communicate.

children.title: REST
children.short_overview: An architectural style using HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) over resource-shaped URLs, with each request self-contained (stateless).

sections.what: An architectural style using HTTP verbs (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) over resource-shaped URLs, with each request self-contained (stateless).
sections.how: This project's Customer app exposes REST endpoints (GET /customers/{id}, POST /customers) using Spring Boot's @RestController.

children.title: GraphQL
children.short_overview: A query language letting a client request exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, resolved server-side by field-level resolvers instead of fixed endpoint shapes.

sections.what: A query language letting a client request exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, resolved server-side by field-level resolvers instead of fixed endpoint shapes.
sections.how: Trades REST's simple caching/tooling for flexible, precise queries — better suited when clients have very different data needs (e.g. mobile vs. web) than when one shape serves everyone.

children.title: Contracts
children.short_overview: An explicit, versioned agreement (types, required/optional fields, error shapes) between an API and its callers, checked mechanically rather than left as a mutual assumption.

sections.what: An explicit, versioned agreement (types, required/optional fields, error shapes) between an API and its callers, checked mechanically rather than left as a mutual assumption.

children.title: Validation
children.short_overview: Rejecting a malformed or unsafe request before it reaches business logic, with a clear error rather than a confusing downstream failure.

sections.what: Rejecting a malformed or unsafe request before it reaches business logic, with a clear error rather than a confusing downstream failure.
sections.how: This project's Customer entity uses Jakarta Bean Validation (spring-boot-starter-validation) to reject invalid input at the boundary.

children.title: Versioning
children.short_overview: How an API evolves without breaking existing callers — via URL path (/v2/...), header, or strictly-additive changes only.

sections.what: How an API evolves without breaking existing callers — via URL path (/v2/...), header, or strictly-additive changes only.

children.title: Idempotency
children.short_overview: A request that can be safely retried without causing a second effect — critical for any client that might resend a request after a timeout (was it applied or not?).

sections.what: A request that can be safely retried without causing a second effect — critical for any client that might resend a request after a timeout (was it applied or not?).
sections.how: Typically implemented via a client-supplied idempotency key the server deduplicates on, or by designing the operation itself to be naturally repeatable (e.g. 'set X to 5' vs. 'add 5 to X').

children.title: Error Handling
children.short_overview: Returning a specific, actionable error (status code + machine-readable reason) instead of a generic failure, so a caller (human or another system) can react correctly.

sections.what: Returning a specific, actionable error (status code + machine-readable reason) instead of a generic failure, so a caller (human or another system) can react correctly.
sections.how: This project's own qa-evaluator explicitly requires a specific failure reason to reach the caller (e.g. RepoToolError re-raised as MCP's ToolError) rather than a generic message — the same principle applied to AI tool design as to API design.

children.title: Networking
children.short_overview: The layers a request travels through between a client and a server, and where each kind of failure/latency actually happens.

children.title: DNS
children.short_overview: Translates a hostname (e.g. agentic-platform-backend-production.up.railway.app) into an IP address before any connection can be made — the first, often-overlooked point of failure or latency.

sections.what: Translates a hostname (e.g. agentic-platform-backend-production.up.railway.app) into an IP address before any connection can be made — the first, often-overlooked point of failure or latency.
sections.how: This project hit a real DNS failure: a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel registered successfully at the edge but its hostname never resolved in public DNS — confirmed via direct queries to Cloudflare's own resolver, not guessed.

children.title: TCP
children.short_overview: A reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport protocol underlying HTTP — establishes a connection (three-way handshake) before any data flows.

sections.what: A reliable, ordered, connection-oriented transport protocol underlying HTTP — establishes a connection (three-way handshake) before any data flows.

children.title: TLS
children.short_overview: Encrypts and authenticates a connection (the 'S' in HTTPS) using a certificate proving the server's identity — a custom domain isn't fully live until its own certificate is provisioned.

sections.what: Encrypts and authenticates a connection (the 'S' in HTTPS) using a certificate proving the server's identity — a custom domain isn't fully live until its own certificate is provisioned.
sections.how: This project's custom domain (agentic.karthikdevadoss.com) had its DNS configured but certificate provisioning was still pending — directly observed via a real TLS handshake failure (SEC_E_WRONG_PRINCIPAL), not assumed.

children.title: HTTP
children.short_overview: The application-layer protocol (request/response, methods, status codes, headers) almost all web APIs are built on.

sections.what: The application-layer protocol (request/response, methods, status codes, headers) almost all web APIs are built on.
sections.how: Every route in this project's own Starlette backend (agent/web_server.py) and Spring Boot Customer app is an HTTP handler.

children.title: Proxy
children.short_overview: An intermediary that forwards requests on behalf of a client or server — used for caching, load balancing, TLS termination, or reaching a network the client can't reach directly.

sections.what: An intermediary that forwards requests on behalf of a client or server — used for caching, load balancing, TLS termination, or reaching a network the client can't reach directly.
sections.how: This project reached its own event-ledger Postgres instance over a public TCP proxy (Railway's private DATABASE_URL isn't reachable from a laptop), and Cloudflare/ngrok tunnels were used as reverse proxies for temporary public access.

children.title: Load Balancer
children.short_overview: Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances for capacity and fault tolerance — not currently needed at this project's single-instance scale.

sections.what: Distributes incoming requests across multiple server instances for capacity and fault tolerance — not currently needed at this project's single-instance scale.

children.title: Timeout
children.short_overview: An explicit limit on how long to wait for a response before giving up — without one, a hung dependency can hang every caller indefinitely.

sections.what: An explicit limit on how long to wait for a response before giving up — without one, a hung dependency can hang every caller indefinitely.
sections.how: This project found a real bug where the Target Application panel could load forever because fetch() has no built-in timeout — fixed with an explicit Promise.race 8-second timeout.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: Re-attempting a failed request, usually with backoff, when the failure is likely transient — must be paired with idempotency to be safe.

sections.what: Re-attempting a failed request, usually with backoff, when the failure is likely transient — must be paired with idempotency to be safe.
sections.how: This project's event ledger retries a failed remote insert via a local outage spool with idempotent (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING) retry, so a retry can never create a duplicate row.

children.title: Compute
children.short_overview: The runtime resources (processes, threads, CPU, memory) a program actually executes on.

children.title: Process
children.short_overview: An OS-level unit of execution with its own memory space — this project's Spring Boot app and its Python agent run as separate processes.

sections.what: An OS-level unit of execution with its own memory space — this project's Spring Boot app and its Python agent run as separate processes.

children.title: Thread
children.short_overview: A unit of execution within a process, sharing its memory — Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat handles each HTTP request on its own thread by default.

sections.what: A unit of execution within a process, sharing its memory — Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat handles each HTTP request on its own thread by default.

children.title: CPU
children.short_overview: The physical resource actually executing instructions — a bottleneck when work is computation-heavy (e.g. embedding generation) rather than I/O-bound.

sections.what: The physical resource actually executing instructions — a bottleneck when work is computation-heavy (e.g. embedding generation) rather than I/O-bound.

children.title: Memory
children.short_overview: RAM available to a process — a JVM's heap size, or a Python process's working set, both bounded by real memory the host actually has.

sections.what: RAM available to a process — a JVM's heap size, or a Python process's working set, both bounded by real memory the host actually has.

children.title: JVM
children.short_overview: The Java Virtual Machine — compiles Java bytecode to native execution, manages memory (heap/garbage collection) and threading for this project's Spring Boot Customer app.

sections.what: The Java Virtual Machine — compiles Java bytecode to native execution, manages memory (heap/garbage collection) and threading for this project's Spring Boot Customer app.
sections.how: This project's app/ directory is a real Spring Boot 4.1.1 / Java 17 application running on a real JVM, compiled and tested via Maven (mvnw).

children.title: Concurrency
children.short_overview: Multiple logical tasks making progress over the same time period — via threads, async I/O, or separate processes — each with different tradeoffs for shared-state safety.

sections.what: Multiple logical tasks making progress over the same time period — via threads, async I/O, or separate processes — each with different tradeoffs for shared-state safety.
sections.how: This project's Starlette backend uses async request handlers plus background threads (for run execution) and a lock-guarded background sync trigger for the event ledger spool, to avoid blocking the fast synchronous telemetry path.

children.title: Databases
children.short_overview: Systems of record for persistent, structured data — how it's stored, queried, and kept consistent.

children.title: Relational DB
children.short_overview: Stores data in tables with defined schemas and relationships, queried via SQL — this project uses H2 (in-memory, for the Customer app demo) and Postgres (durable, for the event ledger).

sections.what: Stores data in tables with defined schemas and relationships, queried via SQL — this project uses H2 (in-memory, for the Customer app demo) and Postgres (durable, for the event ledger).

children.title: Oracle
children.short_overview: A widely-used enterprise relational database — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A widely-used enterprise relational database — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: JDBC
children.short_overview: Java's standard low-level API for connecting to and querying a relational database — JPA is built on top of it.

sections.what: Java's standard low-level API for connecting to and querying a relational database — JPA is built on top of it.
sections.how: Spring Data JPA (used by this project's Customer app) uses JDBC underneath via Hibernate.

children.title: JPA
children.short_overview: Java Persistence API — an ORM standard mapping Java objects to relational rows, implemented here by Hibernate via Spring Data JPA.

sections.what: Java Persistence API — an ORM standard mapping Java objects to relational rows, implemented here by Hibernate via Spring Data JPA.
sections.how: This project's Customer entity/CustomerRepository use Spring Data JPA directly.

children.title: Transactions
children.short_overview: A group of database operations that either all succeed or all roll back together (ACID) — prevents a partial, inconsistent write from ever being visible.

sections.what: A group of database operations that either all succeed or all roll back together (ACID) — prevents a partial, inconsistent write from ever being visible.

children.title: Indexing
children.short_overview: A data structure (typically a B-tree) letting the database find rows without scanning the whole table — the standard fix for a slow query on a large table.

sections.what: A data structure (typically a B-tree) letting the database find rows without scanning the whole table — the standard fix for a slow query on a large table.

children.title: Connection Pooling
children.short_overview: Reuses a fixed set of already-open database connections across requests instead of opening/closing one per request — opening a real DB connection is expensive.

sections.what: Reuses a fixed set of already-open database connections across requests instead of opening/closing one per request — opening a real DB connection is expensive.
sections.how: Spring Boot defaults to HikariCP as its connection pool whenever spring-boot-starter-data-jpa is on the classpath, as it is in this project's Customer app, even without explicit pool configuration.

children.title: Replication
children.short_overview: Copying a database's data to one or more additional nodes for read scaling and/or failover — not used in this project's current single-instance setup.

sections.what: Copying a database's data to one or more additional nodes for read scaling and/or failover — not used in this project's current single-instance setup.

children.title: Partitioning
children.short_overview: Splitting a large table's data across multiple physical segments (by range, hash, etc.) so no single segment grows unbounded — a scale technique this project's current data volume doesn't yet need.

sections.what: Splitting a large table's data across multiple physical segments (by range, hash, etc.) so no single segment grows unbounded — a scale technique this project's current data volume doesn't yet need.

children.title: Caching
children.short_overview: Storing a cheap-to-read copy of expensive-to-compute or expensive-to-fetch data, at the cost of it potentially going stale.

children.title: Redis
children.short_overview: An in-memory key-value store commonly used for caching, sessions, and pub/sub — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: An in-memory key-value store commonly used for caching, sessions, and pub/sub — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Cache-Aside
children.short_overview: The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the real source, then populates the cache for next time — the most common caching pattern.

sections.what: The application checks the cache first; on a miss, it reads the real source, then populates the cache for next time — the most common caching pattern.

children.title: TTL
children.short_overview: Time-to-live — an expiration after which a cached value is considered stale and must be refreshed, bounding how wrong a cache can be.

sections.what: Time-to-live — an expiration after which a cached value is considered stale and must be refreshed, bounding how wrong a cache can be.

children.title: Invalidation
children.short_overview: Actively removing/updating a cached value the moment its source changes, rather than waiting for TTL expiry — famously one of the two hard problems in computer science.

sections.what: Actively removing/updating a cached value the moment its source changes, rather than waiting for TTL expiry — famously one of the two hard problems in computer science.
sections.how: This project's own PDF book cache (learn_pdf.py) invalidates by content hash of the canonical Learn tree rather than a fixed TTL, so a stale book is never served after Learn content genuinely changes.

children.title: Consistency
children.short_overview: How quickly and reliably a cache's value matches its underlying source of truth after a write — a real tradeoff against caching's whole performance benefit.

sections.what: How quickly and reliably a cache's value matches its underlying source of truth after a write — a real tradeoff against caching's whole performance benefit.

children.title: Distributed Systems
children.short_overview: Systems whose components run on separate machines/processes and communicate over an unreliable network — different failure assumptions than a single process.

children.title: Availability
children.short_overview: The fraction of time a system successfully responds to requests — often traded against consistency under network partition (CAP theorem).

sections.what: The fraction of time a system successfully responds to requests — often traded against consistency under network partition (CAP theorem).

children.title: Consistency
children.short_overview: Whether every reader sees the same (and most recent) data at the same time — strong consistency is expensive across a network; many real systems choose eventual consistency deliberately.

sections.what: Whether every reader sees the same (and most recent) data at the same time — strong consistency is expensive across a network; many real systems choose eventual consistency deliberately.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: See System Design -> Networking -> Retry — the same idempotency-paired principle applies across service boundaries.

sections.what: See System Design -> Networking -> Retry — the same idempotency-paired principle applies across service boundaries.

children.title: Idempotency
children.short_overview: See System Design -> APIs -> Idempotency — critical at scale, since network partitions make 'did that request actually land?' a routine question, not an edge case.

sections.what: See System Design -> APIs -> Idempotency — critical at scale, since network partitions make 'did that request actually land?' a routine question, not an edge case.

children.title: Queues
children.short_overview: A durable buffer decoupling a producer from a consumer, so the consumer can process work at its own pace and survive being temporarily down.

sections.what: A durable buffer decoupling a producer from a consumer, so the consumer can process work at its own pace and survive being temporarily down.

children.title: Kafka
children.short_overview: A distributed, partitioned, replicated log used as a high-throughput event streaming/queueing backbone — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A distributed, partitioned, replicated log used as a high-throughput event streaming/queueing backbone — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Event-Driven Architecture
children.short_overview: Components react to events (facts that already happened) rather than being directly called — this project's own event ledger is a lightweight, single-table instance of the same core idea (append-only, consumers read from it independently).

sections.what: Components react to events (facts that already happened) rather than being directly called — this project's own event ledger is a lightweight, single-table instance of the same core idea (append-only, consumers read from it independently).
sections.how: agent/event_ledger.py's delivery_events table is an append-only log every part of this platform (Dashboard, Usage, Learn's knowledge-candidate pipeline) reads from independently, rather than services calling each other directly.

children.title: Security
children.short_overview: Protecting a system's data, identity, and actions from unauthorized access or use.

children.title: Authentication
children.short_overview: Verifying who is making a request (login, tokens, API keys) — not yet implemented anywhere in this project's own Customer app (explicitly out of scope so far).

sections.what: Verifying who is making a request (login, tokens, API keys) — not yet implemented anywhere in this project's own Customer app (explicitly out of scope so far).

children.title: Authorization
children.short_overview: Deciding what an already-authenticated identity is allowed to do — distinct from authentication, and the concept this project's risk_policy.py applies to AI actions rather than human identities (what is this agent allowed to auto-execute).

sections.what: Deciding what an already-authenticated identity is allowed to do — distinct from authentication, and the concept this project's risk_policy.py applies to AI actions rather than human identities (what is this agent allowed to auto-execute).
sections.how: agent/risk_policy.py deterministically gates auto-execution by risk/complexity, structurally separate from the reasoning it gates — the same 'authorization is a separate deterministic decision' principle as classic app authorization.

children.title: JWT
children.short_overview: A signed, self-contained token (JSON Web Token) commonly used to carry identity/claims between services without a shared session store — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A signed, self-contained token (JSON Web Token) commonly used to carry identity/claims between services without a shared session store — not used anywhere in this project's own code; general knowledge only.

children.title: Spring Security
children.short_overview: Spring's authentication/authorization framework — not used in this project's Customer app (no auth layer implemented yet); general knowledge only.

sections.what: Spring's authentication/authorization framework — not used in this project's Customer app (no auth layer implemented yet); general knowledge only.

children.title: Cognito
children.short_overview: AWS's managed identity/user-pool service — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

sections.what: AWS's managed identity/user-pool service — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

children.title: FusionAuth
children.short_overview: A self-hostable identity/auth server — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

sections.what: A self-hostable identity/auth server — not used anywhere in this project; general knowledge only.

children.title: Secrets
children.short_overview: Credentials/keys that must never be committed, logged, or exposed to a model's output — this project actively enforces this (redact_secrets(), .env gitignored, key rotation after one real exposure).

sections.what: Credentials/keys that must never be committed, logged, or exposed to a model's output — this project actively enforces this (redact_secrets(), .env gitignored, key rotation after one real exposure).
sections.how: tools.redact_secrets() deterministically redacts credential-shaped values before anything reaches a log, trace, or the event ledger — applied at the shared boundary so every consumer benefits automatically.

children.title: Least Privilege
children.short_overview: Granting only the access actually needed for a task, nothing more — this project's qa-evaluator subagent is a direct application: Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/WebFetch only, Write/Edit explicitly disallowed.

sections.what: Granting only the access actually needed for a task, nothing more — this project's qa-evaluator subagent is a direct application: Read/Glob/Grep/Bash/WebFetch only, Write/Edit explicitly disallowed.
sections.how: `.claude/agents/qa-evaluator.md`'s disallowedTools (Write/Edit/NotebookEdit) enforces least privilege structurally for an AI subagent, the same principle as scoping a service account's IAM permissions.

children.title: Reliability
children.short_overview: Keeping a system correct and available in the presence of real failures, not just under ideal conditions.

children.title: Failure Modes
children.short_overview: The specific, enumerable ways a system can go wrong — naming them explicitly (timeout vs. crash vs. wrong-data vs. partial-success) is what makes them detectable and preventable rather than a vague 'something broke'.

sections.what: The specific, enumerable ways a system can go wrong — naming them explicitly (timeout vs. crash vs. wrong-data vs. partial-success) is what makes them detectable and preventable rather than a vague 'something broke'.

children.title: Retry
children.short_overview: See Networking -> Retry.

sections.what: See Networking -> Retry.

children.title: Timeout
children.short_overview: See Networking -> Timeout.

sections.what: See Networking -> Timeout.

children.title: Circuit Breaker
children.short_overview: Stops calling a dependency that's already failing repeatedly, for a cooldown period, instead of piling up more failing/slow calls on top of an already-struggling system.

sections.what: Stops calling a dependency that's already failing repeatedly, for a cooldown period, instead of piling up more failing/slow calls on top of an already-struggling system.

children.title: Requested-Effect Verification (Production Verification)
children.short_overview: The practice of confirming a deployed change's SPECIFIC requested observable effect is genuinely live in production — not merely that a server responds, or that a deploy command exited 0.

sections.what: The practice of confirming a deployed change's SPECIFIC requested observable effect is genuinely live in production — not merely that a server responds, or that a deploy command exited 0.
sections.why: HTTP 200 and 'deployment succeeded' both prove the server is reachable, not that the requested content is there. Skipping this step is exactly how a false success gets reported to a human.
sections.how: Capture the exact expected new content (e.g. the literal new file bytes) before deploying. After the deploy is believed active, independently fetch the real production endpoint and compare against that captured expectation — not a paraphrase, not a status code. Only mark the change COMPLETED/verified when the comparison matches.
sections.when: Any time a system deploys or applies a change autonomously and needs to report success/failure to a human or another system. Unnecessary for read-only investigation with no mutation.
sections.real_experience: Real incident: Workbench run trainer-7769757e reported 'Deployment: VERIFIED (HTTP 200)' and claimed a footer changed to requested text, but the real Customer App still showed the OLD footer — the deploy-wait loop had exited early on a Railway CLI 'Online' signal that actually described the PREVIOUS deployment still serving traffic while the new one built in the background. Fixed in agent/web_server.py::_decide_deployment_outcome and the VERIFYING PRODUCTION polling loop: production is now polled directly for the exact expected content (agent/web_server.py's run.trainer_expected_content) for up to 15 minutes, and COMPLETED requires BOTH reachability AND content match.
development_steps: Observed: Workbench UI showed VERIFIED but real production had old content.
Investigated event ledger for the real run (never guessed) — found content_changed_from_baseline=false was captured but unused by the decision function.
Root-caused the deploy-wait loop's premature exit on a Railway CLI text signal that doesn't distinguish OLD-still-serving from NEW-active.
Fixed _decide_deployment_outcome to require content_verified, not just HTTP 200.
Added regression tests reproducing the exact false-positive scenario.
Re-verified live with a real public acceptance run.
failure_modes: A CLI status text ('Online') can describe a stale deployment, not the one you just triggered.
Never treat 'the deploy command succeeded' as equivalent to 'the change is live'.

interview.question: How do you know a deployment actually worked?
interview.short_answer: Never trust HTTP 200 or a CLI exit code alone — independently fetch the real endpoint and check for the specific content you expected to change.
interview.deep_answer: Deployment transport success (the server is reachable, the deploy command exited 0) is a different claim from software-change success (the requested behavior is actually live). We had a real incident where a Workbench run reported 'VERIFIED' based on HTTP 200 while the old content was still being served — root cause was a CLI status signal describing a stale, still-serving deployment. The fix: capture the exact expected new content before deploying, then independently re-fetch production and do a real comparison — never a status code — before reporting success.
interview.real_incident_story: run trainer-7769757e claimed a footer change was live; the Customer App still showed the old text. The deploy had genuinely completed in the background moments later — the bug was in when and how we checked, not in the deploy itself.

children.title: Rollback
children.short_overview: Reverting to a known-good prior version when a deployment is found to be bad — requires that prior version to actually still be deployable/available.

sections.what: Reverting to a known-good prior version when a deployment is found to be bad — requires that prior version to actually still be deployable/available.

children.title: Recovery
children.short_overview: Restoring correct operation after a failure — for data, this means a tested restore path, not just a backup that has never been proven to actually restore.

sections.what: Restoring correct operation after a failure — for data, this means a tested restore path, not just a backup that has never been proven to actually restore.
sections.how: This project's event ledger has a manual on-demand portable backup that has exported real rows successfully, but a restore has explicitly NOT yet been tested — an honestly-tracked open gap, not assumed solved.

children.title: Observability
children.short_overview: Being able to answer 'what is this system actually doing right now, and what did it just do' from real captured evidence, not from guessing.

children.title: Logs
children.short_overview: Discrete, timestamped records of what happened — this project's own safe trace (tool name, sanitized input, status) is a deliberately narrow log designed to never leak secrets or file contents.

sections.what: Discrete, timestamped records of what happened — this project's own safe trace (tool name, sanitized input, status) is a deliberately narrow log designed to never leak secrets or file contents.

children.title: Durable Append-Only Event Ledger
children.short_overview: A single canonical, append-only Postgres table capturing every observable engineering event (model calls, tool calls, proposals, approvals, builds, tests, commits, deployments, human interventions) with a stable envelope schema.

sections.what: A single canonical, append-only Postgres table capturing every observable engineering event (model calls, tool calls, proposals, approvals, builds, tests, commits, deployments, human interventions) with a stable envelope schema.
sections.why: Before this existed, every observable event lived only in one process's memory and a small local gitignored log — a crash or a lost laptop meant losing all history. Historical trajectories cannot be reconstructed after the fact if never captured.
sections.how: One table (infra/event-ledger/schema.sql), a canonical envelope (event_id, timestamp, event_type, run_id, source, activity_class, provider/model/token columns, a JSONB payload for event-specific data), write-through inserts the moment each event happens (never batched), idempotent via ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on event_id, with a local outage spool as a fallback so an insert failure never drops an event.
sections.when: Any system where 'what actually happened, in order, with evidence' needs to survive process restarts, crashes, or feed future analysis/evals — not needed for a purely stateless, disposable computation with no need to reconstruct history.
sections.real_experience: Built as the project's declared #1 near-term priority ('durability first'). Additive design proved itself repeatedly: new event types (repository_workspace_check, run_usage_summary, and this session's v2_trial events) were added without any schema migration, just new event_type strings and JSONB payload shapes — because the schema was designed with a flexible payload column from the start.
development_steps: Chose Railway Postgres (already-trusted provider) over introducing a new datastore.
Designed one canonical envelope instead of a table per event type.
Wired write-through recording into every real event emission point.
Added an outage-safe local spool + idempotent retry.
Backfilled historical local logs with clear reconstructed-evidence tagging, never mixed with live-observed events.
failure_modes: A field only ever written into JSONB payload (never a dedicated column) is invisible to any query that selects columns directly — a real bug found this session when run_usage_summary's real cost data wasn't reaching a dashboard that queried columns.

interview.question: How would you design durable observability for an agentic system?
interview.short_answer: One append-only table, one flexible envelope with a JSONB payload for event-specific fields, write-through inserts, idempotent by event_id, with an outage spool as a fallback — never batch-at-end.
interview.deep_answer: The core design decision is capturing broadly with provenance now and interpreting later — raw evidence that isn't captured at the moment it happens can never be reconstructed. One canonical envelope avoids table-per-event-type proliferation while a payload JSONB column lets new event types be added additively, with zero migrations, as long as the shape is a JSON object. Idempotent inserts (ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING on a UUID event_id) make retries after an outage safe. The real lesson from operating this: don't let a field live ONLY in the payload if a downstream query needs to select on or aggregate it directly.
interview.real_incident_story: A dashboard economics section showed 'NOT CAPTURED YET' even though real cost data existed the whole time in run_usage_summary events — because that data lived only inside the JSONB payload, and the dashboard's hardcoded display never queried the ledger at all. Root cause was two bugs stacked: a stale hardcoded UI plus a real column-vs-payload gap.
