children.title: System Design: Capacity Estimation & Back-of-Envelope Math
children.short_overview: The concrete arithmetic (QPS, storage, bandwidth) that turns a vague 'design X at scale' prompt into a specific, defensible architecture.

sections.why: Nearly every System Design interview explicitly rewards doing real, if approximate, capacity math before proposing an architecture — it's the single clearest signal separating a candidate who can justify their design choices with numbers from one who's pattern-matching to a memorized architecture diagram regardless of the actual scale implied by the prompt.
sections.history_evolution: 'Back-of-envelope' estimation as a named engineering practice traces to physicist Enrico Fermi's famous habit of estimating physical quantities (like the Trinity test's blast yield, from paper drifting in the shockwave) using only rough numbers and reasoning chains — the same 'Fermi estimation' approach was adopted into software capacity planning as systems grew large enough that provisioning decisions needed justification before being built. It became a standard, explicit part of the tech-industry System Design interview format as those interviews formalized in the 2010s (popularized in written form by resources like 'System Design Interview' by Alex Xu, 2020).
sections.why_now: Needed the moment a design decision (how many database replicas, whether to shard, whether caching is even necessary) depends on actual expected load — skipping this step and jumping straight to 'we'll use microservices and Kafka' regardless of whether the system serves 10 or 10 million users per day is a common, easily-avoided interview and real-world mistake.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: the proposed architecture is sized to the business's actual (or realistically projected) scale — neither so small it will fall over immediately, nor so large it wastes budget solving a problem the business doesn't have yet. NFR: explicit, numeric targets for QPS, latency, storage growth, and bandwidth, derived from stated or reasonably-assumed business inputs (daily active users, actions per user, average payload size), not left as vague adjectives.
sections.design_intellect: The core idea is that a small number of derived numbers (average QPS, peak QPS via a peak-to-average multiplier, storage growth per year, bandwidth) determine which architectural techniques are actually necessary — caching is only worth discussing once read QPS is shown to be high; sharding is only worth discussing once single-node storage or write-throughput limits are shown to be approached; a load balancer is only meaningfully justified once a single server's estimated capacity is shown to be insufficient for peak QPS. Deriving these numbers first, then letting them drive the design, is what separates principled System Design from architecture-by-buzzword.
sections.how_exactly: Given a stated or assumed business input (e.g. '10 million daily active users, each performs 5 actions/day') -> total daily actions = DAU x actions/day (50 million) -> average QPS = total daily actions / 86,400 seconds (~580 QPS) -> peak QPS is estimated by applying a peaking factor (commonly 2-3x average, adjusted for known traffic patterns like time-zone concentration or event-driven spikes) giving a peak design target (~1,200-1,700 QPS) -> storage estimate: (average payload size per action) x (total actions per day) x (retention period in days) gives raw storage growth, which then informs replication factor and database/partitioning strategy -> these numbers then directly justify (or rule out) specific techniques: e.g. a single well-provisioned database instance can often handle far more QPS than candidates assume, meaning premature sharding is a common over-engineering mistake revealed by actually doing the math.
sections.low_level_internals: These estimates connect directly to real hardware limits worth knowing approximate orders of magnitude for: a single modern SSD read is on the order of ~100 microseconds; an L1 cache reference ~1 nanosecond, RAM reference ~100 nanoseconds, a same-datacenter network round trip ~0.5 millisecond, a cross-continent round trip ~100-150 milliseconds (the widely-cited 'latency numbers every programmer should know,' originally compiled by Jeff Dean and Peter Norvig at Google) — knowing these orders of magnitude is what lets a candidate sanity-check whether a proposed design's latency budget is even physically plausible.
sections.who: The System Design candidate/engineer doing the estimation, informed by realistic assumptions about the business (DAU, actions per user, payload sizes) either given in the prompt or explicitly stated as an assumption, since a wrong-but-explicitly-stated assumption is far better than an unstated one.
sections.industry: Every major tech company's System Design interview format explicitly allocates time for and rewards capacity estimation before architecture proposal; it's considered a baseline, table-stakes skill for mid-to-senior backend roles, not an advanced/optional topic.
sections.business: Correctly-sized capacity planning directly controls infrastructure cost — provisioning for an imagined 'web scale' when actual traffic is orders of magnitude smaller wastes real money every month, while under-provisioning risks an outage at exactly the moment of business success (a product going viral, a marketing campaign landing).
sections.product: A product's actual usage pattern (bursty vs. steady, read-heavy vs. write-heavy) directly determines which parts of a design need investment — capacity estimation is the bridge between 'what the product does' and 'what the system must be built to handle.'
sections.cost_economics: This entire topic is fundamentally a cost-optimization discipline: every architectural technique (caching, sharding, replication, CDN) has a real infrastructure and complexity cost, and capacity estimation is what justifies (or rules out) paying that cost for a given system's actual scale.
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: a proposed System Design in an interview (or a real architecture in production) includes complex scaling techniques (sharding, multi-region replication) with no numeric justification, and separately fails to account for a specific bottleneck (e.g. a single component's realistic single-node capacity) that the actual estimated load would have revealed. Diagnosis (interview context): the interviewer probes 'how many requests per second do you expect this to handle' and the candidate has no answer, or the design doesn't change based on the answer once given. Root cause: skipped or superficial capacity estimation. Fix: always derive QPS/storage/bandwidth numbers early, from stated or explicitly-assumed inputs, and let those numbers drive (and be visibly referenced by) every subsequent design decision. Business impact (real-world): either wasted infrastructure spend from unjustified over-engineering, or a genuine capacity-driven outage from under-provisioning that correct estimation would have flagged in advance.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: Rigorous, stated-assumption-based estimation (defensible, shows real engineering judgment, takes a few minutes of interview time) vs. skipping estimation and defaulting to a 'standard' scalable architecture regardless of actual scale (faster, but reveals pattern-matching rather than reasoning, and is a common way candidates lose credibility in a System Design interview) vs. over-precise estimation chasing exact figures (wastes interview time on decimal-point precision when the actual goal is correct order-of-magnitude reasoning).

interview_mode.sec_15: Before proposing an architecture, derive rough average and peak QPS, storage growth, and bandwidth from the given (or explicitly assumed) business scale — these numbers should visibly drive which techniques (caching, sharding, load balancing) are actually justified.
interview_mode.sec_30: State assumptions explicitly (DAU, actions per user, payload size), derive average QPS by dividing daily actions by seconds-per-day, apply a peaking factor for the design target, and estimate storage growth from payload size times daily volume times retention — then reference these numbers when justifying every subsequent architecture decision, rather than defaulting to a fixed 'scalable' pattern regardless of actual scale.
interview_mode.min_2: Walk a full example (e.g. 10M DAU, 5 actions/day) through average QPS, peak QPS, and storage estimation, explicitly stating each assumption, then show how the resulting numbers determine whether caching/sharding/a CDN are actually justified for this specific scale versus overkill.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Cite the 'latency numbers every programmer should know' (L1 cache ~1ns, RAM ~100ns, SSD read ~100us, same-datacenter round trip ~0.5ms, cross-continent round trip ~100-150ms) to sanity-check whether a proposed design's latency budget is physically plausible.
interview_mode.system_design: This is the opening move of nearly every System Design interview — do it first, explicitly, before any component diagram, and revisit the numbers whenever proposing a scaling technique to justify it's actually needed at this scale.
interview_mode.business_value: Frame over-engineering (unjustified complexity for the actual scale) and under-provisioning (an outage at the worst possible moment) as two symmetric, equally real cost mistakes that correct estimation avoids.

sections.current_status_2026: The core Fermi-estimation methodology and the 'latency numbers every programmer should know' reference figures remain unchanged and are still the standard baseline cited in System Design interviews and preparation material in 2026; what has shifted is that many candidates now also need to estimate AI/LLM-inference-related capacity (tokens/sec, context-window memory, GPU/accelerator throughput) using the same fundamental estimation discipline applied to a newer class of resource.

children.title: CAP Theorem & PACELC
children.short_overview: Why a distributed system can't have perfect consistency, availability, and partition tolerance simultaneously, and the more complete PACELC framing of what's actually traded even when there's no partition.

sections.why: CAP theorem is one of the most commonly cited (and commonly oversimplified/misquoted) pieces of distributed-systems vocabulary in System Design interviews — being able to state it precisely, and go a level deeper with PACELC, is a clear signal of real understanding versus repeating a slogan.
sections.history_evolution: Eric Brewer conjectured CAP informally in a 2000 keynote; Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch formally proved it as a theorem in 2002. It states that a distributed data system can provide at most two of Consistency (every read sees the latest write), Availability (every request receives a non-error response), and Partition tolerance (the system continues operating despite network partitions between nodes) — but since network partitions are a real, unavoidable possibility in any real distributed system, the practical reading is that a system must choose, specifically during a partition, between consistency and availability (partition tolerance isn't really optional to give up). Daniel Abadi's 2010 PACELC extension pointed out CAP only describes behavior during a partition, and added the else clause: even when there's no partition, a system still trades Latency against Consistency during normal operation, which is arguably the more common, everyday trade-off engineers actually face.
sections.why_now: Relevant whenever designing or choosing a distributed data store (a database, cache, or coordination service spanning multiple nodes/regions) and deciding how it should behave when nodes can't communicate, or how much latency to pay for stronger consistency during normal operation. Irrelevant for a single-node system with no network partition possible at all.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement: understand explicitly, for a given feature, whether a stale read (an availability-favoring choice) or a rejected/failed request during a partition (a consistency-favoring choice) is more acceptable to the business — this decision should be made deliberately per use case, not assumed. Architecture: this framing directly explains why some databases (Postgres, traditional RDBMS in single-region config) default to strong consistency while others (Cassandra, DynamoDB) default to high availability with eventual consistency, and why the 'right' choice genuinely depends on the specific data and use case.
sections.design_intellect: The core idea CAP formalizes is that consistency and availability are fundamentally in tension the moment nodes can't communicate — you can either refuse to serve a request you can't guarantee is consistent (favoring C) or serve it anyway using potentially-stale local data (favoring A), but you cannot do both simultaneously during an actual partition. PACELC's addition (the 'else' — latency vs. consistency even without a partition) captures the day-to-day reality that achieving strong consistency across nodes even in normal operation requires coordination (e.g. waiting for a quorum of replicas to acknowledge a write) that costs real latency, which is why even a system 'choosing CP' still has an explicit, tunable latency cost during entirely normal operation.
sections.how_exactly: A write is submitted to a distributed data store with multiple replicas -> if the system prioritizes consistency (CP, or PC in PACELC terms), the write waits for acknowledgment from a quorum (or all) of replicas before returning success, and a read similarly may need to check multiple replicas or route to a designated leader to guarantee it sees the latest value -> if the system instead prioritizes availability (AP, or PA), the write can succeed by being accepted on just one (or a minority of) replicas, and a subsequent read might be routed to a different replica that hasn't yet received that write, returning a stale value -> during an actual network partition (some nodes unable to reach others), a CP system will refuse requests it can't guarantee consistency for (returning an error rather than a possibly-wrong answer), while an AP system will continue answering from whatever locally-available data it has, accepting the risk of inconsistency until the partition heals and replicas reconcile.
sections.low_level_internals: Achieving strong consistency across replicas typically requires a consensus protocol (Raft or Paxos) to agree on write ordering before acknowledging success — this fundamentally requires multiple network round trips between nodes before a write can be confirmed, which is the concrete mechanism behind PACELC's latency cost. An AP system instead often uses conflict resolution strategies applied after the fact (last-write-wins based on timestamps, vector clocks, or CRDTs — conflict-free replicated data types specifically designed so concurrent, independently-applied updates can always be merged deterministically without coordination).
sections.who: The distributed database/coordination service's own replication and consensus layer (implementing the actual CP or AP behavior), the application developer (choosing which data store and consistency level fits each specific use case), and, during an actual partition, the network itself (the physical cause of the trade-off becoming unavoidable rather than theoretical).
sections.industry: CAP theorem is close to universally known vocabulary in backend/distributed-systems interviews, but PACELC is specifically what separates a candidate who's memorized the CAP acronym from one who understands the everyday latency/consistency trade-off that applies even without any partition ever occurring.
sections.business: Choosing AP for data where staleness is genuinely unacceptable (e.g. an account balance, an inventory count near zero) risks real business-impacting inconsistency; choosing CP for data where availability matters far more than perfect freshness (e.g. a social media 'like' count, a product view count) needlessly sacrifices availability/latency for a precision the business doesn't actually need — the correct choice is data-specific, not a single global architectural decision.
sections.product: Users generally tolerate a slightly stale 'like count' far better than an unavailable page, and generally prefer an outright error over confidently displaying a wrong bank balance — product judgment about which failure mode is more acceptable for each specific piece of data is what should drive the underlying consistency-model choice, not a one-size-fits-all default.
sections.cost_economics: Achieving strong consistency has a direct latency cost (quorum round trips) that translates to either accepted higher latency or the infrastructure cost of minimizing it (e.g. keeping replicas geographically close) — an explicit trade to make deliberately per data type rather than defaulting to maximum consistency (and its latency cost) everywhere.
sections.failure_incident: Symptom: during a network partition between regions, a globally-distributed inventory system either (a) shows two customers in different regions both successfully reserving the last unit of stock (an AP system's staleness cost realized) or (b) becomes fully unavailable for purchases in one region even though that region's local replica is healthy (a CP system's availability cost realized). Diagnosis: identifying which trade-off the system's chosen consistency model actually makes, and whether that matches the business's actual tolerance for this specific data, reveals whether the incident is 'working as designed but wrongly chosen' versus a genuine bug. Root cause: often not a bug at all, but a consistency-model choice made without deliberately considering this specific failure mode and its business cost. Fix: for genuinely business-critical exact-count data, move to a CP model (or add a reconciliation/compensation step, as in the Saga pattern, to correct AP-model staleness after the fact) — the fix is a deliberate architecture decision, not a code patch. Business impact: either oversold inventory (a real AP-model cost) or lost sales from unnecessary unavailability (a real CP-model cost) — both are genuine, quantifiable business costs of the underlying trade-off, not something a fix eliminates entirely.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: CP systems (traditional RDBMS in a single primary configuration, ZooKeeper/etcd for coordination — strong consistency, unavailable during a partition affecting the primary) vs. AP systems (Cassandra, DynamoDB in default configuration, most CDNs — always available, eventually consistent) vs. tunable-consistency systems (Cassandra's per-query consistency level, DynamoDB's optional strongly-consistent reads — letting each specific query choose its own point on the trade-off, the most flexible but also most complex-to-reason-about option).

interview_mode.sec_15: CAP theorem says a distributed system can't have perfect consistency, availability, and partition tolerance all at once — since partitions are unavoidable in practice, the real choice is between consistency and availability specifically during a partition.
interview_mode.sec_30: PACELC extends this: even without any partition, a system still trades latency against consistency during entirely normal operation, since strong consistency requires coordination (a consensus protocol like Raft/Paxos) that costs real round-trip time — this everyday latency/consistency trade-off is arguably more relevant to daily engineering decisions than the partition-specific CAP trade-off alone.
interview_mode.min_2: State CAP and PACELC precisely, then give one CP example (a bank balance, correctly rejecting a request during a partition rather than risking an inconsistent read) and one AP example (a social 'like' count, correctly staying available with eventual consistency) to show the choice is data-specific, not a single global architecture decision.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Explain the mechanism behind the latency cost of strong consistency (a consensus protocol needing a quorum round trip before acknowledging a write) versus how AP systems resolve conflicting concurrent writes after the fact (last-write-wins, vector clocks, or CRDTs).
interview_mode.system_design: Use this explicitly to justify per-data-type consistency-model choices within one System Design answer, rather than picking a single database/consistency level for the entire system.
interview_mode.business_value: Tie the choice directly to which failure mode (stale data vs. unavailability) the specific business use case can actually tolerate — this is a product/business judgment call the engineer should surface explicitly, not silently decide alone.

sections.current_status_2026: Distributed SQL databases (CockroachDB, Google Spanner, YugabyteDB) that aim to provide strong consistency with high availability using synchronized clocks and consensus at global scale remain an active, growing area of the industry in 2026, often discussed in System Design interviews as a modern attempt to push the practical trade-off boundary rather than eliminate it entirely — CAP/PACELC's fundamental trade-offs still apply underneath.

children.title: System Design Interview Methodology
children.short_overview: The repeatable structure (clarify -> estimate -> high-level design -> deep dive -> trade-offs) that turns an open-ended prompt into a strong, complete answer.

sections.why: A System Design interview is deliberately open-ended and time-boxed; candidates with strong technical knowledge still fail it by diving into a solution before clarifying the actual problem, or by never revisiting the high-level design once details emerge — having an explicit, rehearsed methodology is what prevents wasting the limited time on the wrong thing.
sections.history_evolution: The System Design interview format itself grew out of large tech companies' need (starting prominently at Google, Amazon, and Facebook in the 2000s-2010s) to assess a candidate's ability to handle genuinely ambiguous, large-scale engineering problems that a coding interview alone can't reveal. The now-standard structured approach (clarify requirements, estimate scale, propose high-level design, deep-dive on 1-2 components, discuss trade-offs/bottlenecks) was consolidated and popularized in written form through widely-used preparation resources (Alex Xu's 'System Design Interview' book series, 2020 onward, and Grokking-style courses), turning what was previously tribal, unwritten interviewer expectation into an explicit, teachable framework.
sections.why_now: Applicable specifically to the interview format itself, and directly transferable to real architecture decision-making at work (an ADR, a design-review document) — the same discipline of clarifying requirements and scale before committing to a design is good practice regardless of whether it's being evaluated in an interview.
sections.big_picture: Business requirement (of the interview itself): demonstrate the ability to take an ambiguous, large-scale problem from unclear requirements to a defensible, scale-appropriate architecture within a fixed time budget, communicating reasoning clearly throughout — the interviewer is evaluating the *process*, not just the final diagram.
sections.design_intellect: The core idea is sequencing: clarify functional and non-functional requirements and explicitly state assumptions first (since designing before understanding the actual problem wastes the most expensive resource in the interview — time, and risks solving the wrong problem entirely); estimate scale next (since scale numbers determine which techniques are even relevant, per Capacity Estimation); propose a high-level design only once both of those are established, using simple, labeled boxes and data flow; then deep-dive into the 1-2 components the interviewer signals most interest in, rather than shallowly covering everything; and close with trade-offs, bottlenecks, and how the design evolves at 10x scale, which demonstrates the meta-skill of knowing a design's own limits.
sections.how_exactly: Interviewer states an intentionally vague prompt (e.g. 'design a URL shortener' or 'design a notification system') -> candidate spends the first several minutes asking clarifying questions (read vs. write ratio, expected scale, consistency requirements, what's explicitly out of scope) and states any unclarified assumptions explicitly -> candidate performs a quick capacity estimation (QPS, storage) from the now-clarified inputs -> candidate proposes a high-level architecture (client, API layer, database, cache, any async components) as a simple diagram, narrating the data flow for the core use case -> interviewer typically steers toward a specific area of interest (e.g. 'how do you handle the ID-generation collision problem' or 'how does this scale to 10x traffic') -> candidate deep-dives into that specific component with real technical depth -> candidate proactively discusses trade-offs made, what would break first at significantly higher scale, and how the design would evolve.
sections.low_level_internals: Not applicable in the traditional CPU/memory sense — the 'internals' of this topic are the meta-cognitive process itself: allocating interview time deliberately (a common rough split is roughly 5-10 minutes clarify/estimate, 15-20 minutes high-level design, 15-20 minutes deep dive, 5-10 minutes trade-offs/wrap-up, adjusted to interviewer signals throughout) rather than letting the conversation drift.
sections.who: The candidate (driving the structure and communicating reasoning aloud throughout, since silent thinking is invisible to an evaluator), and the interviewer (providing an intentionally ambiguous prompt and steering focus toward whichever areas they want deeper evaluation of).
sections.industry: This exact structure is now explicitly taught and expected across the industry for mid-to-staff-level backend/full-stack interviews at essentially every major tech employer; deviating from it (e.g. skipping clarification entirely) is one of the most commonly cited reasons strong engineers still fail a System Design round.
sections.business: In a real job (not just the interview), the same discipline (clarify requirements and scale before committing to an architecture) is what prevents building the wrong system or over/under-engineering for a misunderstood scale — the interview format is testing a genuinely transferable professional skill, not an artificial game.
sections.product: Explicitly connecting a design decision back to a stated product/business requirement during the interview (e.g. 'since read latency matters more than perfect consistency for this feature, I'd choose eventual consistency here') signals product-aware engineering judgment, a specific thing senior-level interviewers look for beyond raw technical correctness.
sections.cost_economics: A candidate who proactively discusses the cost/complexity trade-off of each proposed technique (rather than reflexively proposing the most complex, 'impressive'-sounding architecture regardless of the stated scale) signals senior/staff-level judgment specifically because real engineering decisions are always cost-constrained, not judged on technical sophistication alone.
sections.failure_incident: Symptom (interview failure mode): a candidate immediately proposes a fully-scaled, complex microservices/Kafka/sharded-database architecture for a prompt whose clarified scale turns out to be small, or never revisits their initial design once new requirements emerge partway through. Diagnosis: this reads to an interviewer as pattern-matching to a memorized 'impressive' architecture rather than reasoning from the actual stated problem, and as inflexibility once new information arrives. Root cause: skipped or superficial requirements clarification, and treating the high-level design as fixed once drawn rather than as a living hypothesis to revise. Fix: always clarify and estimate before designing, and explicitly state when new information changes an earlier design choice rather than silently ignoring the conflict. Business impact (real-world analog): the identical mistake made for real, at work, produces an architecture mismatched to the business's actual scale and needs — the interview format specifically screens for this because it's a genuinely costly real mistake.
sections.alternatives_tradeoffs: A rigid, memorized template applied mechanically regardless of the specific prompt (safe but can feel scripted and fails to adapt when the interviewer steers in an unexpected direction) vs. a flexible internalized structure (clarify -> estimate -> design -> deep-dive -> trade-offs) applied with judgment about how much time each deserves for this specific prompt and this specific interviewer's signals — the latter is what genuinely strong candidates demonstrate.

interview_mode.sec_15: Structure a System Design answer as: clarify requirements and state assumptions, estimate scale, propose a high-level design, deep-dive where the interviewer signals interest, then discuss trade-offs and how the design evolves at higher scale — in that order, since each step's output feeds the next.
interview_mode.sec_30: The single most common way strong engineers fail this interview format is skipping clarification and diving straight into a solution, or over-designing for a scale that was never actually established — the methodology exists specifically to prevent both, and its real value (clarify before designing) transfers directly to real architecture decisions at work, not just the interview.
interview_mode.min_2: Walk the full structure with a concrete example prompt (e.g. a URL shortener), showing what clarifying questions to ask, what a quick capacity estimate looks like, and how to keep the high-level design revisable as the interviewer steers toward a deep dive.
interview_mode.deep_technical: Not the natural fit for this topic — pivot instead to whichever specific technical deep-dive the interviewer is steering toward (capacity estimation, a specific distributed-systems pattern, etc.), since this topic is itself about structuring that pivot well.
interview_mode.system_design: This topic *is* the System Design interview's own meta-structure — state it explicitly and follow it, narrating the structure aloud ('let me first clarify a few requirements before proposing anything') so the interviewer can see the process, not just the end result.
interview_mode.business_value: Explicitly connect at least one design decision back to a stated business/product requirement during the walkthrough, to demonstrate the six-lens (not purely technical) judgment senior/staff interviews specifically probe for.

sections.current_status_2026: The clarify -> estimate -> design -> deep-dive -> trade-offs structure remains the standard, industry-wide expected format in 2026; a growing number of System Design interviews now also explicitly include an AI/LLM-serving component (e.g. 'design a system that serves an AI chat feature at scale'), requiring the same estimation and architecture discipline applied to token throughput, model-serving latency, and GPU/accelerator capacity alongside classic web-scale concerns.

domains.title: AI-Assisted Software Engineering
domains.short_overview: How to build software WITH AI agents responsibly: what the AI should decide vs. execute, how to define success before implementation starts, how to independently verify results, and how to recognize and prevent AI failure modes.

children.title: Acceptance Contracts (Define Success Before Coding)
children.short_overview: A small, machine-readable definition of what 'done' means for a change — requirement, target, expected observable effect, required deterministic gates, allowed terminal outcomes — captured BEFORE any implementation starts.

sections.what: A small, machine-readable definition of what 'done' means for a change — requirement, target, expected observable effect, required deterministic gates, allowed terminal outcomes — captured BEFORE any implementation starts.
sections.why: Without an explicit contract, 'did this work?' gets answered by whoever implemented it, using whatever criteria occur to them after the fact — exactly the condition that produces false-success reports.
sections.how: A small schema (agent/acceptance_contract.py: requirement_id, requirement_text, target_application, expected_observable_effect, required_gates, allowed_terminal_outcomes, evidence_requirements) with a validate() that rejects a contract whose success criterion isn't independently checkable, and cross-checks that referenced gates/outcomes are real things the runtime can actually produce.
sections.when: Any autonomous or semi-autonomous change where success needs to be judged by someone/something other than the implementer. Overkill for a one-line change a human reviews directly with full context.
sections.real_experience: Designed and standalone-tested (agent/test_acceptance_contract.py, 7/7 passing) — not yet wired into the live Workbench pipeline. Used for real in both V2 shadow trials: each trial's contract explicitly required an EXACT expected string, which is precisely what let Trial #2's evaluator catch a one-character seeded defect.
development_steps: Identified the false-success incident as a symptom of undefined success criteria.
Designed the smallest useful schema, not a general workflow engine.
Added a validate() that checks the contract itself for a checkable success criterion.
Cross-checked allowed_terminal_outcomes against the real runtime's TERMINAL_RUN_STATES via a test — proving the two can never silently drift apart.

interview.question: How do you prevent an AI agent from grading its own homework?
interview.short_answer: Write down exactly what 'done' means, in a checkable form, before the agent starts — then have someone/something else check the real evidence against that definition, not the agent's own report.
interview.deep_answer: An Acceptance Contract makes the success criterion an artifact that exists independently of the implementation, created before any code is written. The critical design point is that the contract's own validator rejects vague or unverifiable success criteria — a requirement like 'the page looks better' isn't acceptable; 'the response contains this exact string' is. This doesn't replace independent evaluation — it's the input to it.
interview.real_incident_story: In Shadow Trial #2, the contract explicitly demanded an EXACT string. A seeded one-character capitalization defect ('Find A Customer' vs the required 'Find a Customer') would have been easy to wave away as 'close enough' without that exactness requirement — the evaluator caught it precisely because the bar was unambiguous.

children.title: Independent QA Evaluation (The Implementer May Not Certify Itself)
children.short_overview: A second, genuinely separate reasoning process that checks a proposed change's real evidence against its Acceptance Contract — without access to the implementer's own claims, reasoning trace, or self-assessment.

sections.what: A second, genuinely separate reasoning process that checks a proposed change's real evidence against its Acceptance Contract — without access to the implementer's own claims, reasoning trace, or self-assessment.
sections.why: Self-evaluation by the same agent/context that did the work tends toward optimism — it already believes its own reasoning was sound. Anthropic's own harness research and this project's own real incident both point the same direction: separating generator from evaluator improves reliability, especially exactly where self-evaluation is weakest.
sections.how: A distinct subagent definition (.claude/agents/qa-evaluator.md) with restricted tools (read/test/fetch only, no Write/Edit), given ONLY the Acceptance Contract and pointers to real evidence — never told the implementer's claimed outcome. It re-runs or re-reads deterministic checks itself (re-fetch, re-compile, re-read source) rather than trusting any prior report, and returns PASS/FAIL/UNKNOWN.
sections.when: Worth the extra cost/latency when a false positive is genuinely costly (production changes, security-relevant code, anything reported to a human as fact) and the task is hard enough that self-evaluation is known to be unreliable. Not worth it for trivial, easily-human-checked changes.
sections.real_experience: Built and run three times (V2 Shadow Trials #1-#3). A real, honest limitation was found and later resolved: the custom subagent type was not recognized as a native subagent_type in two long-running sessions that predated/outlived its creation (ACT-006) — worked around transparently in Trials #1-#2 by having a general-purpose agent read and follow qa-evaluator.md verbatim, clearly labeled as not-native. A genuinely fresh Claude Code v2.1.268 session (Trial #3) confirmed native invocation works with no workaround: the subagent self-identified its role, used only its allowed tools, and returned real independently-gathered evidence. Trial #2 proved the concept concretely: the evaluator caught a deliberately seeded, subtle defect (a capitalization mismatch) with byte-exact verification. Trial #3 attempted to test a harder property — refusing to guess (UNKNOWN) under genuinely insufficient evidence — and surfaced a subtler lesson about contract design instead (see 'evaluator-uncertainty-and-verdict-design').
development_steps: Designed the subagent with an explicit 'may not certify its own production success' non-negotiable rule for the IMPLEMENTER, and a symmetric independence rule for the evaluator itself.

Trial #1: ran a correct change through the evaluator — PASS, with real independent re-verification (re-fetch, re-compile, re-read source), plus one valuable unprompted process question about commit-gating semantics.
Trial #2: seeded exactly one controlled, harmless defect after a correct implementation, withheld this from the evaluator entirely, and confirmed it returned FAIL with exact matching evidence.
ACT-006 fresh-session probe: confirmed native subagent_type='qa-evaluator' registration works with zero workaround.

Trial #3: designed a 2-criterion contract intending to elicit UNKNOWN; the evaluator instead correctly reasoned that a verifiably-absent required artifact is conclusive FAIL evidence, not an unknowable gap — a genuine, useful safety property (it never fabricated the missing evidence to force a verdict either way), even though it didn't test the originally-intended capability.
failure_modes: Native subagent definitions may not be visible to a session that was already running when the definition file was added — RESOLVED: verified fixed in a genuinely fresh session (ACT-006 closed 2026-09-11).

The evaluator's own token/cost usage is only available as an AGGREGATE_ONLY total per subagent invocation (Agent tool task-notification: total tokens/tool_uses/duration_ms) — no input/output/cache/cost decomposition is exposed by Claude Code's hook interface (verified by inspecting claude_code_hook.py's own documented hook-field list). Now at least durably recorded per actor_role in the event ledger (subagent_usage_summary events) rather than lost to conversation scrollback.

Designing a contract that reliably elicits UNKNOWN is harder than it looks — a 'required evidence is missing' criterion must be unreachable/unrulable by ANY of the evaluator's tools, not just 'the expected artifact isn't there' (see evaluator-uncertainty-and-verdict-design).

interview.question: Why not just let the same agent that made the change verify it?
interview.short_answer: Because it already believes its own reasoning — an independent evaluator with no access to the implementer's claims, checking real evidence itself, catches what self-review structurally can't.
interview.deep_answer: This mirrors an ordinary code-review principle (a reviewer shouldn't approve their own PR) applied to AI agents specifically because LLM self-evaluation has a documented tendency toward leniency. The design choices that make this actually work: (1) genuine context separation, so the evaluator never inherits the implementer's framing of the problem; (2) the evaluator re-does real checks itself instead of trusting reported results; (3) evidence requirements are defined by the Acceptance Contract in advance, so the evaluator can't quietly loosen the bar to reach a comfortable verdict.
interview.real_incident_story: In a controlled trial, we corrected a heading to 'Find a Customer', then secretly changed it to 'Find A Customer' before showing the evaluator anything. It independently fetched the live page, ran `cat -A` to check for hidden characters, and correctly reported FAIL — never told a defect existed or where.

children.title: Designing for UNKNOWN: When an Evaluator Should Refuse to Guess
children.short_overview: The design discipline of writing acceptance criteria so that a genuinely unresolvable evidence gap produces UNKNOWN, distinct from a criterion whose non-satisfaction is itself conclusively provable (which should produce FAIL, not UNKNOWN).

sections.what: The design discipline of writing acceptance criteria so that a genuinely unresolvable evidence gap produces UNKNOWN, distinct from a criterion whose non-satisfaction is itself conclusively provable (which should produce FAIL, not UNKNOWN).
sections.why: An evaluator that always forces PASS/FAIL is unsafe (it will eventually guess PASS on a real failure). But an evaluator is also useless if it says UNKNOWN every time evidence for a criterion isn't sitting in front of it — the distinction that matters is whether the criterion's truth is independent of anything the evaluator's own tools could ever observe or rule out, versus whether the evaluator can conclusively rule it out (e.g. proving an artifact was never created, anywhere in history).
sections.how: Classify each acceptance criterion by evidentiary reachability before implementation starts: (1) DIRECTLY CHECKABLE (read a file, run a command) — PASS/FAIL only; (2) CONCLUSIVELY RULE-OUT-ABLE (an artifact's total absence, provable by exhaustive search e.g. across all of git history) — still PASS/FAIL, absence is real evidence; (3) GENUINELY UNREACHABLE (depends on an external system/credential/observation the evaluator's tool set can never reach, or on a fact that leaves no artifact trail either way) — this is the only category where UNKNOWN is the correct default, and the evaluator should say so explicitly rather than silently treating 'I found nothing' as proof of absence.
sections.when: Whenever designing or benchmarking an independent-evaluator system, and whenever writing an Acceptance Contract for a real change where some criterion might not be provable one way or the other within the evaluator's actual access (e.g. a claim about production traffic behavior when the evaluator has no monitoring access, or a compliance claim needing a document that may or may not exist outside the repository).
sections.real_experience: V2 Shadow Trial #3 (2026-09-11) tried to elicit UNKNOWN with a contract requiring a human-logged browser-confirmation file. The qa-evaluator correctly searched the ENTIRE git history (not just the working tree) for that path, found it had never existed, and concluded FAIL — a conclusively rule-out-able criterion (category 2 above), not a genuinely unreachable one (category 3). This was the right call by the evaluator, but the wrong experiment by the trial designer: it re-tested 'does the evaluator avoid fabricating evidence,' which Trial #2 already covered, rather than 'does the evaluator recognize the limits of its own tools.'
development_steps: Designed Trial #3's contract intending category-3 uncertainty.
Implementer satisfied the checkable criterion, correctly declined to fabricate the unreachable one.
Evaluator ran an exhaustive absence-check (git log --all) rather than a shallow one, correctly reclassifying the criterion as conclusively provable, not merely unobserved.
Result was a well-evidenced FAIL, not UNKNOWN — analyzed post-hoc as a category mismatch in contract design, not an evaluator defect.

Recorded the categorization framework above so a future Trial #4 can design a genuine category-3 criterion (e.g., a claim resting on a production system the evaluator has no credentials to reach at all).
failure_modes: An 'evidence is missing' benchmark is not automatically a test of refusing-to-guess — check whether the evaluator could, in principle, conclusively rule the criterion out with the tools it has. If yes, FAIL/PASS is correct behavior, not UNKNOWN.

A rigorous evaluator will search more thoroughly than a benchmark designer expects (exhaustive git history, not just the working tree) — design uncertainty around what is fundamentally unreachable, not around what merely takes effort to rule out.

interview.question: How do you design an AI evaluator that knows when to say 'I don't know'?
interview.short_answer: Distinguish criteria the evaluator can conclusively rule out (including by proving an artifact was never created) from criteria that depend on something genuinely outside its tools' reach — only the second category should produce UNKNOWN.
interview.deep_answer: It's tempting to treat 'the expected evidence isn't in front of me' as automatic grounds for UNKNOWN, but that conflates 'I haven't looked hard enough' with 'this cannot be known.' A rigorous evaluator should exhaust the reasonable means available to it (e.g., searching full history, not just the current state) before concluding something is unknowable — and if that exhaustive check conclusively proves absence, that's evidence for FAIL, not grounds for UNKNOWN. Genuine UNKNOWN belongs to criteria whose truth is independent of anything the evaluator's tools could ever observe, such as a claim about a system it has no access to at all.
interview.real_incident_story: We built a trial expecting UNKNOWN by requiring a human-logged confirmation file that we knew didn't exist. The evaluator searched the full git history, proved the file had never existed on any ref, and correctly called it FAIL. We initially thought we'd disproven the evaluator's judgment; re-analysis showed the evaluator was right and our trial design was the flawed part — a valuable lesson in how much harder it is to construct genuine irreducible uncertainty than it first appears.

children.title: Skills and Subagents (Claude Code)
children.short_overview: Skills are reusable, on-demand instruction sets loaded when relevant to a task (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md). Subagents are separate-context workers with their own restricted tool access, invoked for a focused, independent task (.claude/agents/<name>.md).

sections.what: Skills are reusable, on-demand instruction sets loaded when relevant to a task (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md). Subagents are separate-context workers with their own restricted tool access, invoked for a focused, independent task (.claude/agents/<name>.md).
sections.why: Without Skills, procedural knowledge (how we verify production changes, what testing states mean, what a QA evaluator must never do) has to be re-derived or re-explained every session. Without subagents, there's no way to get a genuinely separate reasoning context for independent evaluation.
sections.how: Both are GA (general availability) Claude Code features as of version 2.1.267, verified via official documentation rather than assumed from memory. Skills need only `name` + `description` frontmatter; subagents add `tools`/`disallowedTools` for capability restriction. Full Agent Teams (multiple concurrent, peer-communicating sessions) is a separate, still-experimental feature requiring explicit opt-in.
sections.when: Skills: whenever the same procedural knowledge would otherwise be re-explained across sessions or re-derived from scratch. Subagents: when a task genuinely needs isolated context or a restricted capability set. Agent Teams: only once a measured need for concurrent, debating agents is established — not by default.
sections.real_experience: Created 5 project Skills (requirement-contract, implement-small-change, test-change, production-verify, incident-analysis) and one qa-evaluator subagent this session, each scoped to a single stated duty with explicit 'must not' boundaries and references to canonical existing code/docs rather than duplicated knowledge. Deliberately did NOT enable Agent Teams — confirmed experimental and disabled by default via direct documentation verification, and no measured need for concurrent agents exists yet for this project's actual workload.
development_steps: Verified current Claude Code capability formats via a dedicated research subagent WebFetching official docs, rather than trusting recalled/memorized syntax.

Classified existing pipeline responsibilities into deterministic-stays-code vs. agentic-judgment BEFORE writing any Skill, to avoid converting a deterministic gate into an LLM prompt merely because Skills are the new mechanism.
Wrote each Skill to reference canonical sources (e.g. 'see agent/risk_policy.py') rather than restating rules that could drift out of sync with the actual code.
failure_modes: A custom subagent added mid-session is not necessarily visible as a subagent_type to a session that was already running when the file was created — confirmed empirically twice, tracked as ACTION_QUEUE ACT-006, worked around transparently rather than silently faked as native.

interview.question: When would you reach for a Skill vs. a subagent vs. a full multi-agent team?
interview.short_answer: Skill for reusable procedural knowledge in the same context; subagent when you need genuinely separate context or a restricted tool set; a full agent team only once concurrent, peer-communicating agents solve a real, measured problem plain subagents can't.
interview.deep_answer: These three mechanisms trade off cost and isolation differently. A Skill costs nothing extra in context isolation — it's just loaded knowledge in the same reasoning process, appropriate for organizing what's already true. A subagent is a genuinely separate context, at the cost of a new invocation and no shared reasoning trace — the right tool exactly when that separation is the point, as with an independent evaluator. Full Agent Teams add concurrent, peer-communicating sessions, at meaningfully higher token/coordination cost, and current guidance (both official and this project's own constitution's non-attachment-to-architecture principle) is: adopt only once evidence shows a real need, not because it's available.
interview.real_incident_story: We deliberately did not enable Agent Teams for two consecutive controlled trials, using a single independent evaluator subagent instead — which was sufficient to prove the core hypothesis (an independent evaluator catches what self-evaluation misses) without the added cost and experimental-feature risk of full concurrent teams.

children.title: AI Token/Cost Economics and Accounting
children.short_overview: Capturing and aggregating REAL (never estimated post-hoc) token usage and USD cost per AI-driven run, from the actual API response's own usage field, using a versioned pricing table so historical cost never silently changes when prices change later.

sections.what: Capturing and aggregating REAL (never estimated post-hoc) token usage and USD cost per AI-driven run, from the actual API response's own usage field, using a versioned pricing table so historical cost never silently changes when prices change later.
sections.why: Without real capture, cost is invisible until a bill arrives with no way to attribute it. Without a versioned pricing table, a past run's recorded cost can silently become wrong when prices are updated. Without ledger-backed aggregation, a UI can show 'not captured' even when the underlying data has existed the whole time — a real bug this project hit directly.
sections.how: Capture real usage the moment an API response returns (never scraped from a UI counter). Calculate cost via a small versioned pricing module keyed by (provider, model), storing which pricing_version applied. Aggregate from the durable event ledger — the canonical historical source — rather than an in-memory counter that resets on restart or a separate, disconnected display constant.
sections.when: Any system making real, billed API calls that needs to answer 'how much did this cost' at the individual-run, hourly, daily, or lifetime level, especially when the answer needs to survive process restarts.
sections.real_experience: Built agent/pricing_config.py (versioned pricing verified against the live official Anthropic pricing page) and agent/estimation.py (pre-run estimate, clearly labeled ESTIMATED, from historical comparable runs) in an earlier task. This session found and fixed a REAL fragmentation bug: a Dashboard economics section had been hardcoded to 'NOT CAPTURED YET' since before real capture code existed, and was never updated afterward — even though the real ledger had genuine cost data (including the Creator's own observed example: 31,573 input / 2,797 output tokens / 5 API calls) the entire time. A second, deeper bug compounded it: the run_usage_summary event type stored its real cost/token data only inside a JSONB payload field, never in the dedicated queryable columns other usage events use — invisible to any column-based query.
development_steps: Investigated the Creator's reported contradiction by directly querying the live event ledger, not by re-reading UI code first.
Found the real cost/token data existed exactly where reported, confirming the capture layer was correct.
Traced the display bug to a static, years-stale (in project-time) constant that predated the capture code and was never wired to it.
Found the second, compounding bug: JSONB-payload-only storage for one specific event type, invisible to column-based queries.
Fixed both: real columns now populated for that event type, plus a genuine ledger-backed aggregation function (last run / last hour / today / lifetime) replacing the hardcoded constant.
Wrote tests proving both pre-fix (payload-only) and post-fix (column-populated) rows aggregate correctly, so no historical data was orphaned by the fix.
failure_modes: A generic event-recording bridge that doesn't know an event type's specific fields will silently leave those fields as JSONB-only, invisible to any query selecting real columns — extend the bridge per-event-type when a new type carries data that needs to be queryable directly.
A 'known limitation' comment in code/docs needs to be re-checked and corrected once the limitation is actually fixed — an accurate comment left stale after code changes becomes a lie by omission.

interview.question: How do you track real cost for an AI-driven system, and what goes wrong if you don't design it carefully?
interview.short_answer: Capture real usage from the API response itself, price it with a versioned table so history never silently changes, and aggregate from a durable ledger rather than an in-memory counter or a hand-maintained UI constant.
interview.deep_answer: The subtle failure mode we actually hit wasn't missing capture — it was capture existing correctly while the DISPLAY layer stayed disconnected from it, plus one event type storing its data somewhere a standard column-based query couldn't see. Both bugs are instances of the same root problem: a data path that works for the common case (most events populate real columns) silently breaking for an edge case (one event type didn't), with no test catching it because the bug was in the wiring between capture and display, not in either half alone.
interview.real_incident_story: The Creator observed a real run showing captured tokens directly, while a Dashboard elsewhere in the same product still said 'NOT CAPTURED YET' for the same kind of data. Both bugs were real and root-caused from the actual live database, not guessed — the hardcoded Dashboard constant, and a JSONB-payload-only storage gap for one specific event type.

children.short_overview: The explicit division between what a human owns and what an AI may execute within delegated authority, and the four distinct mechanisms (approval, interruption, clarification, escalation) governing when a human must be involved.

children.title: Human Owns
children.short_overview: Purpose, business intent, priorities, budget, architecture boundaries, risk tolerance, security/production authority, ethical boundaries, and final accountability — decisions capability alone does not transfer.

sections.what: Purpose, business intent, priorities, budget, architecture boundaries, risk tolerance, security/production authority, ethical boundaries, and final accountability — decisions capability alone does not transfer.
sections.why: An AI agent can be technically capable of making a change without being the right authority to decide whether that change SHOULD be made — capability is not authority (docs/CONSTITUTION.md).

children.title: AI May Execute Within Authority
children.short_overview: Repository investigation, implementation, bounded refactoring, test generation, evidence collection, documentation, debugging hypotheses, isolated experiments — the HOW, once the human has set the WHAT and WHY.

sections.what: Repository investigation, implementation, bounded refactoring, test generation, evidence collection, documentation, debugging hypotheses, isolated experiments — the HOW, once the human has set the WHAT and WHY.
sections.why: Routine, reversible, well-specified execution work is exactly where delegating to an AI agent creates real leverage without transferring a decision that was never the AI's to make.

children.title: Approval
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes an action exceeds its delegated authority and asks a human before doing it — known in advance, not a reaction to something going wrong.

sections.what: The AI recognizes an action exceeds its delegated authority and asks a human before doing it — known in advance, not a reaction to something going wrong.
sections.why: Capability is not authority: an AI agent can be technically able to do something (deploy, spend budget, touch production) without being authorized to decide that it should, right now, without a human saying yes.
sections.how: A deterministic, code-level gate (not a prompt instruction) decides what needs approval before any agent reasoning happens — this project's risk_policy.py classifies risk/complexity and only then decides auto-execute vs. 'needs Owner authorization', so the same model can't argue its way around the gate.
sections.when: Material ambiguity, destructive/irreversible actions, security-boundary changes, spending above budget authority, production actions with real customer impact.

children.title: Interruption
children.short_overview: A human observes the AI drifting or creating risk mid-run and stops or reorients it — reactive, not planned in advance like approval.

sections.what: A human observes the AI drifting or creating risk mid-run and stops or reorients it — reactive, not planned in advance like approval.
sections.why: Even a well-scoped task can go wrong in ways no upfront gate anticipated — scope creep, a misunderstood requirement, or a tool being used in an unintended way.
sections.how: Requires the human to actually have visibility into what the AI is doing while it's doing it (a live event stream, a visible run log) — interruption is impossible if the only evidence arrives after the fact.
sections.when: When observed behavior diverges from the actual intent, even if no explicit rule was technically broken.

children.title: Clarification
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes its own requirement or context is insufficient to proceed correctly, and asks rather than guessing.

sections.what: The AI recognizes its own requirement or context is insufficient to proceed correctly, and asks rather than guessing.
sections.why: Guessing under genuine ambiguity is exactly the failure mode this project's own AI-guessing-and-failure lessons document repeatedly — a wrong assumption stated confidently is worse than a question.
sections.how: Distinguish 'I could technically proceed with an assumption' from 'the ambiguity materially changes what correct looks like' — only the second genuinely warrants stopping to ask.
sections.when: Requirement text is genuinely ambiguous, evidence needed to proceed correctly doesn't exist yet, or a decision belongs to the human by policy (see Human Role).

children.title: Escalation
children.short_overview: The AI recognizes a decision belongs outside its authority entirely (not just 'I'm unsure', but 'this isn't mine to decide') and routes it to a human rather than acting or even asking a narrow clarifying question.

sections.what: The AI recognizes a decision belongs outside its authority entirely (not just 'I'm unsure', but 'this isn't mine to decide') and routes it to a human rather than acting or even asking a narrow clarifying question.
sections.why: Some decisions (business purpose, ethical boundaries, architecture direction, legal/financial commitments) are categorically the human's to make regardless of how confident or capable the AI is.
sections.how: A recognizable trigger list (see Human Role -> Human Owns) rather than case-by-case judgment calls, so escalation is consistent rather than arbitrary.
sections.when: Business-purpose questions, ethical/dharmic uncertainty, legal/customer commitments, architecture-direction changes, anything the Owner has reserved by policy.

children.title: Human Role, Approval, and Interruption
children.short_overview: The explicit division of what a human owns (purpose, risk tolerance, budget, production/security authority) versus what an AI agent may decide within an authorized boundary — plus the distinct categories of human involvement: approval (known in advance), interruption (human notices drift mid-run), clarification (agent asks because it's uncertain), and escalation (agent detects something outside its authority).

sections.what: The explicit division of what a human owns (purpose, risk tolerance, budget, production/security authority) versus what an AI agent may decide within an authorized boundary — plus the distinct categories of human involvement: approval (known in advance), interruption (human notices drift mid-run), clarification (agent asks because it's uncertain), and escalation (agent detects something outside its authority).
sections.why: Capability does not equal authority. An agent that CAN technically deploy to production, delete data, or spend money doesn't thereby have standing authorization to do so — and asking for approval on every trivial, reversible action causes real approval fatigue that erodes the value of asking at all.
sections.how: A deterministic, text-level risk policy (agent/risk_policy.py) decides auto-execute vs. requires-authorization BEFORE any agent reasoning happens — a keyword/complexity classifier, not an LLM judgment call, precisely because the gate itself must not be gameable by the same reasoning it's gating. Separately, a real approval boundary (agent/execution_tools.py) makes the approve/reject decision structurally unreachable from the model's own tool-calling surface — verified by exact set-membership tests, not a prompt instruction.
sections.when: Risk-based, not uniform: low-risk, reversible, well-specified, sandboxed actions can run without a human in the loop; ambiguous requirements, irreversible actions, secrets, security-boundary changes, and material scope expansion should not.
sections.real_experience: This project's risk_policy.py auto-executes TINY/LOW-risk demo changes (with zero human approvals needed in either V2 shadow trial) while requiring Owner authorization for anything touching security, infrastructure, or larger scope. The approval boundary was proven to fail closed (reject, never silently approve) when no human is present at all — the correct behavior when authority genuinely cannot be reached, not a crash and not a silent yes.
development_steps: Deliberately kept risk classification as plain deterministic code, never an LLM prompt, so the gate can't be argued with by the same model it's gating.

Verified the approval boundary is structurally unreachable from the model (exact set-membership test, not a substring check — an earlier version of this exact test had a false-positive substring bug that was caught and fixed).
Verified fail-closed behavior: a non-interactive environment raises EOFError on an approval prompt; the fix treats 'cannot reach a human' as equivalent to reject, never to approve or to crashing.
failure_modes: A substring check for 'is this forbidden name present' produced a false positive once (matching 'apply_approved_source_change' against a check for 'approve') — exact set-membership checks are required for a security-boundary test to mean what it claims.

interview.question: How do you decide when an AI agent needs human approval?
interview.short_answer: Risk-based, not uniform — gate on reversibility, scope, and ambiguity, decided by deterministic code before any agent reasoning happens, not by asking the agent to judge its own authority.
interview.deep_answer: The key architectural insight is that the GATE deciding auto-execute vs. needs-authorization must itself be deterministic and outside the reasoning it's gating — otherwise you're asking the same system to both propose an action and judge whether it's allowed to. Separately, the actual approve/reject mechanism needs to be structurally unreachable by the model (verified by exact tests, not a prompt instruction saying 'don't call this'), and must fail closed — treating 'no human available' as a rejection, never a default yes.
interview.real_incident_story: A security test asserting 'approve_edit is never exposed as a callable tool' used a substring check and passed even when it shouldn't have, because 'apply_approved_source_change' contains the substring 'approve'. Rewriting it to exact set-membership caught that the test itself had been theater, not a real guarantee.

children.title: Where AI Guesses, and Why It Fails
children.short_overview: The recurring failure modes where an AI agent produces a confident-sounding but wrong claim — usually from an unverified assumption rather than a deliberate lie.

sections.what: The recurring failure modes where an AI agent produces a confident-sounding but wrong claim — usually from an unverified assumption rather than a deliberate lie.
sections.why: Recognizing these patterns is what makes independent verification and deterministic gates necessary in the first place, rather than optional nice-to-haves.
sections.how: Detect by never trusting a claim about system behavior without checking the actual source/runtime; prevent by giving agents the means to check (tools, real environment access) rather than asking them to reason from memory about an unfamiliar codebase or a fast-moving external API.
sections.when: Always relevant wherever an agent reasons about code, APIs, or infrastructure it hasn't directly inspected in the current context.
sections.real_experience: Three real, distinct examples from this project's own recent work: (1) an implementer confidently claimed 'propose_source_change only allows .java files' — false, verified by reading the actual source, root cause was an incomplete prompt, not a real restriction; (2) a Spring Boot 4.1.1 test suite failed to compile against assumed classes (com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper, TestRestTemplate, AutoConfigureMockMvc) that turned out to have moved or not be on the classpath in this exact dependency set — Spring Boot 4 restructured Jackson under a new tools.jackson namespace and split several test-support classes into different modules than in Spring Boot 3.x memory; (3) a seeded one-character capitalization defect was easy to visually skim past without an exact, byte-level check.
failure_modes: Unsupported assumption about a tool's own restriction: verify against the actual source file, not the model's prior turn's own claim.

Wrong library/version assumption: a dependency tree and jar-content inspection settled in minutes what guessing from training-data memory would have gotten wrong (Jackson 3.x's tools.jackson.databind package, not com.fasterxml.jackson.databind, ships with Spring Boot 4.1.1).
Weak/skimmed verification: an exact string comparison (even `cat -A` for hidden characters) catches what a glance does not.

interview.question: Give a real example of an AI agent being confidently wrong, and how you caught it.
interview.short_answer: An implementer claimed a tool restriction that didn't exist in the actual source code — caught by reading write_tools.py directly instead of trusting the claim.
interview.deep_answer: The pattern across all three of our real examples is the same: an agent (or a person, in the Jackson 3 case, reasoning from training-data memory of Spring Boot 3.x) made a plausible-sounding claim about a system it hadn't actually inspected in the current context. The fix is always the same too — go check the real source, the real dependency tree, the real byte content — never accept a claim about system behavior as fact until it's independently verified against the thing itself.
interview.real_incident_story: Writing tests for Spring Boot 4.1.1, `com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper` failed to compile. Instead of guessing at a fix, we ran `mvn dependency:tree` and found Jackson 3.x now ships under `tools.jackson.databind` — a genuine, documented major-version package rename we would not have known about from memory alone.
