children.title: Truthful Testing Terminal States
children.short_overview: An explicit, distinct terminal state for every real testing situation a change can be in: PASSED, FAILED, NOT_APPLICABLE (no test surface exists for this kind of change at all), NOT_CONFIGURED (testing should reasonably apply, but no automated coverage exists yet), and SKIPPED (applicable tests exist but weren't run for this change).

sections.what: An explicit, distinct terminal state for every real testing situation a change can be in: PASSED, FAILED, NOT_APPLICABLE (no test surface exists for this kind of change at all), NOT_CONFIGURED (testing should reasonably apply, but no automated coverage exists yet), and SKIPPED (applicable tests exist but weren't run for this change).
sections.why: Collapsing 'no test files exist yet' into the same label as 'this genuinely can't be tested' hides a real, actionable gap (missing test infrastructure) behind a label that sounds like a deliberate, correct decision.
sections.how: A real, checkable fact decides the state — not a default. If a real test tool was invoked, its actual result is PASSED/FAILED. If not, check whether the changed file type genuinely has no test surface (e.g. a static HTML resource) for NOT_APPLICABLE, whether real test files exist elsewhere in the project but weren't run for SKIPPED (which blocks commit, like FAILED), or otherwise NOT_CONFIGURED (which doesn't block this run, since it's a project-level gap, not this change's fault).
sections.when: Any pipeline that needs to report a testing decision truthfully to a human or another system, especially one that gates further actions (like commit/deploy) on that decision.
sections.real_experience: Real bug found and fixed this session: this project's Workbench was labeling every Java source change as TESTING — NOT APPLICABLE purely because no test files existed yet — semantically wrong, since the Customer app has real testable business logic; the honest label is NOT_CONFIGURED. Fixed alongside writing the project's first real automated tests for that same app (7 tests: a context-load smoke test, 3 service-layer unit tests with a mocked repository, and 3 real HTTP integration tests against the actual running app and database).
development_steps: Identified the semantic bug: 'no test files' was being treated as 'not applicable' unconditionally.
Designed a real decision function keyed off checkable facts: does a test tool result exist, does the changed file have any test surface at all, do test files exist elsewhere in the project.
Wrote regression tests proving each state is reached for the right reason, including that SKIPPED (unlike NOT_CONFIGURED/NOT_APPLICABLE) blocks commit.
Wrote the project's first-ever real Customer app tests, closing part of the actual gap the states now describe honestly.
failure_modes: NO TEST FILES != TESTING NOT APPLICABLE — the two are different claims and must never share a label.

interview.question: What's wrong with a system that reports 'tests not applicable' whenever no tests exist?
interview.short_answer: It conflates 'this genuinely can't be tested' with 'nobody has written tests for this yet' — the second is an actionable gap, not a settled, correct decision, and hiding it behind the first label makes the gap invisible.
interview.deep_answer: The fix requires distinguishing testing states by a real, checkable fact rather than a single boolean. A static HTML resource genuinely has no unit-test surface — NOT_APPLICABLE is honest there. A Java class with real business logic and zero test coverage is a different, actionable situation — NOT_CONFIGURED. And if tests DO exist but weren't run for a specific change, that's SKIPPED, which should block commit exactly like a failure, because unlike the other two, it's not a project-level gap — it's this run's own omission.
interview.real_incident_story: This project's own Workbench was silently mislabeling every Java change with zero test coverage as 'not applicable' — until this session's fix distinguished the states and, in the same pass, wrote the first real automated tests the Customer app has ever had.
